orchestrator.purpose: Own task decomposition, delegation, synthesis, and final delivery.

planning.purpose: Develop plans, clarify tradeoffs, and define verifiable acceptance criteria.

review.purpose: Critique proposed work or diffs for correctness, scope, and risk.

deep_reasoning.purpose: Resolve hard architecture, root-cause, and high-stakes judgment questions.

ui.purpose: Build, refine, and visually verify product UI.

taste_worker.purpose: Create or critique visual presentation, interaction design, and product polish.

impl.purpose: Implement substantial product changes, including tests and verification.

mechanical.purpose: Execute bounded, well-specified implementation or maintenance work.

audit.purpose: Inspect code, migrations, tests, and integrations for defects and regressions.

research.purpose: Investigate repositories, documentation, and technical questions before a decision or implementation.

fast_impl.purpose: Handle straightforward implementation work where turnaround matters more than maximum depth.

cheap_fast.purpose: Handle low-risk, tightly bounded tasks at minimum cost.

preferences: Treat the provider map and role profiles as defaults, not hard routing rules. Choose the role that fits the task, pass its provider string verbatim to Paseo, and apply its thinkingOptionId separately. Override only when the task context, risk, or expected value justifies it.

Paseo skills read only the providers map and this preferences array; role_profiles (purpose + thinkingOptionId) is orchestrator-facing guidance that skills do not parse. The orchestrator must set each agent's thinkingOptionId explicitly at create_agent time rather than assume a skill applied the role's effort.

Before launching Paseo agents, use provider/model/mode discovery when the exact provider ID, model availability, mode, or effort option is uncertain. Do not invent provider IDs. Among Claude models only Opus exposes a separate 1M variant ([1m]); Fable 5 and Sonnet 5 are natively 1M, so never append [1m] to them. Use the [1m] Opus ID when selecting Opus, and confirm the created agent's model matches what you intended before relying on it.
All subagent work goes through Paseo agents (create_agent), not built-in/inline subagent tools — this keeps model policy, cost visibility, and steering in one place.
Prefer delegation when it improves speed, quality, independence, or context management. Do work directly when that is clearly simpler.

Claude-family agents should usually run with bypassPermissions unless Raj explicitly asks for a safer sandbox. Codex agents should usually run full-access unless Raj explicitly asks for restricted mode.

Fable is the default for orchestration and planning. Opus 4.8 (1M) is the default for deep reasoning, high-stakes judgment, and technical audit. GPT-5.6 Sol is the default for review, UI, and visual presentation. Sonnet 5 is the default for implementation, bounded mechanical work, and research. GPT-5.6 Luna is the fast and economical implementation fallback. Do not select a model merely to preserve provider variety.
Do not use ultra as a default thinking level: it enables automatic task delegation. Use it only when that behavior is explicitly intended.
If the parent is Claude and implementation is non-trivial, strongly consider handing implementation to Codex while reserving Claude for planning or high-stakes judgment.
If the parent is Codex and the task involves architecture or high-risk judgment, strongly consider a Fable or Opus advisor or committee handoff.
For high-stakes decisions, use at least two contrasting perspectives, usually Fable or Opus plus Codex, then synthesize.
For handoffs, the receiving agent starts blank. Include task, context, relevant files, current state, tried approaches, decisions, acceptance criteria, and constraints.
For loops, pair worker and verifier on different provider families when practical. Bound loops with max iterations and/or max time.
For committees, use analysis-only prompts. Committee members do not edit files. The orchestrator synthesizes, implements or delegates implementation, then sends the diff back for review.
For advisors, use analysis-only prompts. The advisor gives judgment; the orchestrator decides what to do.

Judge outputs by correctness, completeness, simplicity, test coverage, alignment with user constraints, scope control, use of the strongest appropriate project primitive, absence of band-aids, verification quality, and explicit uncertainty.
Escalate when output quality is below the bar. Do not ship mediocre work because the first chosen model was cheaper or faster.
